Hi everyone, I'm Fritz a research engineer at startup called Ridge AI for AI-native embedded visual analytics.

And we want to talk to you about exploring high-dimensional data across many angle.

---

Talking points (~0:30)
- Introduce the title, then us in one casual sentence each.
- The background loop is the Gaussian blobs preview from dtour.dev. Bundle it into assets/ before the talk so it works offline.

Understanding high-dimensional data is hard. A very common way to visually understand such data are 2D or 3D scatter plots that are based on either a subsample of dimensions in the case of PCA or a an embedding of many dimensions into few. Both approaches are lossy in that they either disregard some dimensions or necessarily introduce distortion and artifacts. Neither is ideal and there's lots of work to avoid hiding information and reduce artifacts but ultimately, it's unavoidable.

Take this example here, showing the same data, Fashion MNIST in this case, on the left we see a PCA representation of the first two components while the rest is hidden, and on the right we see various non-linear embedding plots all based on the same neighborhood graph created with varying levels of attraction / repulsion. Which one is most faithful? There's no general answer. They show different views that, we argue, together enable one to build an understanding of the high-dimensional manifold. So one 2D projection is rarely enough.

---

Talking points (~0:45)
- We usually look at high-dimensional data through one 2D layout from LE, UMAP, t-SNE, etc.
- Those methods sit on an attraction–repulsion spectrum (Böhm et al.). Same data, very different pictures: continuous vs. clustered.
- There are ways around this: reduce distortion, pre-transform the data, visualize where the layout is distorted. Simplest answer: one 2D projection may just not be enough.
- The strip is Fashion MNIST, the same data as the last usage scenario, which sets up the payoff later.

The obvious answer is to use more than just a single 2D projection as the previous slide already showed. But what's most effective to build an understanding of the high-dimensional manifold? Generally, there are three approaches:
1. Show multiple 2D projections in a grid, which results in a well known scatter plot matrices
2. Animate between 2D projections as a movie, which is called a tour
3. Or manually manipulate individual axes

All three have different pros and cons, that can be explained by an axis on freedom of traversal & steerability: where the left side offer no freedom to traverse and steer and the right side offers complete freedom, which comes at the cost of high-information 
- While s

The problem is that that to effectively understand high-dimensional data it'd moving between these modes requires different tools

---

Talking points (~1:30), one per click
- Start: three classic ways to look at many projections, ordered by freedom of traversal. Scatter plot matrix (static, compare at a glance), guided tour (a movie on a fixed path), manual tour (drag axes, full control). Moving between them means switching tools (the arrows).
- Click 1, freedom of traversal: the axis appears under the three modes, from none (static grid) to complete (manual tour).
- Click 2, cognitive load: each step to the right adds load (manual tours are slow and demanding to start). The jumps are where you have to switch tools: the activation energy of switching between disconnected tools and re-finding your points. Say it's a sketch, not data.
- Click 3, guided tour: the GGobi movie plays (Wickham & Cook). You watch, you don't steer.
- Click 4, manual tour: the Distill clip plays (Li, Zhao, Scheidegger), GGobi stops. Full control, one axis at a time.
- Click 5, dtour: one interface spanning all three modes. The classic tools fade into dtour's keyframe gallery, guided tour, and manual tour (clips play on their own). The arrows turn yellow: you move between modes without switching tools.
- Click 6, cognitive load drops: switching costs disappear (no jumps), and starting a manual tour from a promising keyframe also lowers the climb a bit.
- Click 7, Shneiderman's mantra: overview (keyframe gallery) → zoom & filter (scrub, select, color) → details on demand (manual and grand tour). Add freedom only when you need it.
- Click 8: move freely between modes. Every mode shift is animated, so points keep their identity (object constancy). Then switch to the live demo.

Talking points (~2:15)
- Two linked rings in 4D · 500K points · live at dtour.dev.
- Two classes in only 4D, yet the four 2D views in the gallery don't give a good feel for the shape. A nice illustration of the problem.
- Explain the interface on the live widget as you go:
  - (1) Gallery: one preview per keyframe, arranged around a circular slider. Doubles as lookahead and orientation.
  - (2) Guided tour: click a preview, drag the slider, or scroll. The central scatter moves smoothly along the keyframe path.
  - (3) Manual tour: axes become draggable handles. Each handle's length is that dimension's contribution, so it's both a control and a legend.
  - Color by labels and lasso-select points, then follow them across projections (select-then-explore).
- Script: (1) look at the gallery → (2) click a preview → (3) scrub slowly so the rings pass through each other → (4) select one ring → (5) switch to manual and drag an axis → (6) start the grand tour as the closer.

Talking points (~0:45), one per click
- Start: the naive path, geodesic interpolation between consecutive keyframes. Each piece is smooth, but the direction jumps at every keyframe (C⁰). The yellow dots are keyframe projections, and they can be anywhere: dtour is generic.
- Click 1: Catmull–Rom on the frames, re-orthonormalized with Gram–Schmidt, bends the path into a smooth (C¹) curve that still visits every keyframe. No direction jumps.
- Click 2: the guided path is a closed loop, wrapping from the last keyframe back to the first, so it becomes dtour's slider ring. Keyframes sit at their geodesic distance, so they're unevenly spaced.
- Click 3: the slider spaces keyframes equally. Squeezed segments turn thicker, stretched ones thinner, so the ring width encodes the geodesic distance between keyframes.
- Click 4 (play icon): playback moves at constant speed through projection space, so the marker lingers on wide segments.
- Click 5 (hand icon): scrubbing moves evenly around the slider, so the projection travels faster where keyframes are far apart.

Talking points (~0:30)
- dtour accepts any sequence of p×2 orthonormal bases as a tour, so it isn't tied to one tour algorithm.
- Hyperdimensional tours: one high-dimensional space seen from different angles, e.g., the little tour over PCs or our Laplacian Eigenmaps tour. Every in-between frame is a real projection.
- Sequential tours: aligned 2D embeddings of the same points, e.g., sweeping a hyperparameter, or comparing DR methods or embedding models. Only keyframes are real embeddings; the interpolation just keeps object constancy, and dtour flags that visually.
- Bring your own: anything that fits one of the two families plugs right in.
- Next: one live scenario per family. Brain atlas = hyperdimensional (little tour), Fashion MNIST = sequential (attraction–repulsion).

UMAP is capturing real progression confirmed by PCA but it's not immune to optimization or algorithmic artifacts like the disconnected cluster. And it actually lies on a spectrum of neighborhood embedding and there's one hyperparameter parameter of attraction-repulsion (repulsion explains the isolation of "blood")

---

Talking points (~1:15 · live)
- 276K cells, developing mouse brain (La Manno et al.). Little tour over PC1–8 (left), linked to the 2D UMAP of that same PCA space (right).
- UMAP runs on the PCA output, so structure in UMAP but not in any PC pair comes from the non-linear embedding.
- Stable: gastrulation → ectoderm progression shows up in both.
- Split: choroid plexus is one group in PCA, but two islands in UMAP.
- Isolated: blood is an island only in UMAP (repulsion).
- Demo: click a class in the legend or lasso in either view; the selection syncs both ways. Then scrub / press play to see which PC projection separates it.
- Linking is just a few lines in marimo/Jupyter: dtour selection ↔ jupyter-scatter.

And so with dtour we can actually look at this by visualizing a sequence of 2D embeddings along this spectrum that representing LE -> t-SNE

---

Talking points (~1:15 · live)
- 70K Fashion MNIST images, a sequential tour of four keyframes: LE-like (ρ=100) → FA2-like (ρ=30) → UMAP-like (ρ=4) → t-SNE (ρ=1).
- Keyframes are warm-started embeddings, Procrustes-aligned along the exaggeration sweep (Böhm et al.). Only keyframes are real embeddings; in-between frames just help track points.
- Demo: go to the UMAP-like keyframe and lasso the tight cluster of ~96 points among shirts & dresses. The images on the right show they are shorts: compact silhouettes that look like tops.
- Scrub back toward LE: the cluster dissolves, so it's an artifact of repulsion.
- Boundaries (e.g., boot-like bags) stay put across the spectrum → more trustworthy than tightness.

Talking points (~0:20)

- Optional: keep a looping grand tour running in the background during Q&A.
